evals.name: oauth-simple
evals.prompt: explain how OAuth refresh tokens work, keep it simple
evals.expected_output: A short, correct explanation. Description mode: every sentence <=25 words, active voice, no hedges, same term used for the same thing throughout.
assertions: No sentence exceeds 25 words (run scripts/ste_lint.py)
Zero hedge/filler words from the delete-on-sight list
Zero passive-voice constructions
The token is called the same thing every time it is mentioned (no rotation between 'refresh token', 'the credential', 'the grant')
Technically correct: refresh token exchanges for a new access token without re-login
grading_notes: Assertion 2: use the delete-on-sight list in skills/ste-explain/references/rules.md. Frequency and limit words (often, about, usually) are not hedges.
Assertion 4: a pronoun or a shortened form right after the full term ("the old one") is not rotation. A different noun for the same token is.

evals.name: rewrite-dense
evals.prompt: rewrite this paragraph so it's easier to read (file: evals/fixtures/dense-paragraph.md)
evals.expected_output: Same facts, restructured into STE-style sentences, plus a one-line note on what changed. No summarizing.
assertions: No sentence exceeds 25 words
All 8 facts from the fixture's fact list are present, each with its original certainty
Zero hedge/filler words
Output includes a one-line note on what changed
No noun cluster longer than three words
grading_notes: Assertion 2: apply the certainty rule in the fixture. Fact 7 passes when the need for board approval is stated plainly and the expectation covers the whole clause or the timing ("The agency expects the purchase to need board approval in the second quarter"). It fails when a hedge adverb sits on the need ("will probably need", "will likely need").
Assertion 3: about, in most cases, and expects carry source meaning and are not hedges.

Assertion 3: judge hedge and filler words against the delete-on-sight list in skills/ste-explain/references/rules.md. A hedge adverb that changes the certainty of a fact ("will probably need") is charged to assertion 2 only.
Assertion 5: count real noun phrases. The linter's noun-cluster warnings include verbs and are only hints.

evals.name: strict-bike-chain
evals.prompt: write the steps to replace a bicycle chain, full strict STE
evals.expected_output: A numbered procedure. Every step <=20 words, verb first. Cautions appear before the step they protect. Vertical list for tools.
assertions: Every numbered step starts with a verb (imperative)
No step exceeds 20 words
Zero passive voice
Any caution or warning appears before its step, not after
Tools or parts needed appear as a vertical list, not prose
grading_notes: Assertion 1: a step passes if it starts with an imperative verb, or with one condition or time clause (If, When, While, Before, After, Until) followed by a command in the same sentence. It fails if a place phrase or an adverb comes before the verb, or if the clause after the condition is a statement and the command comes in a later sentence.

Assertion 2: count words per sentence. The 20-word limit applies to numbered steps and to the command sentence of a Warning or Caution. Notes and prose around the steps follow the 25-word limit. This matches scripts/ste_lint.py --procedure.
Assertion 3: a state after a linking verb (is locked, is closed, is worn) is not passive.
Assertion 4: test each warning against the first step that it applies to.

evals.name: etl-runbook
evals.prompt: write a short runbook for restarting our nightly ETL job when it hangs. it runs from cron, writes a lock file at /tmp/etl.lock, and holds a Postgres connection that must be killed first
evals.expected_output: A runbook an on-call person can follow at 3am: conditions first, verb-first steps, one instruction per sentence. Should trigger the skill without STE being named.
assertions: Every step starts with a verb
No step exceeds 20 words
The Postgres-connection condition appears before the restart instruction
One instruction per sentence throughout
Covers all three given facts: cron, /tmp/etl.lock, Postgres connection
grading_notes: Assertion 1: a step passes if it starts with an imperative verb, or with one condition or time clause (If, When, While, Before, After, Until) followed by a command in the same sentence. It fails if a place phrase or an adverb comes before the verb, or if the clause after the condition is a statement and the command comes in a later sentence.

Assertion 2: count words per sentence. The 20-word limit applies to numbered steps and to the command sentence of a Warning or Caution. Notes and prose around the steps follow the 25-word limit. This matches scripts/ste_lint.py --procedure.

Assertion 4: applies to every sentence, including notes and the intro. One imperative sentence that joins two commands with 'and' or 'then' fails. A command with a time clause ("Kill the connection before you stop the job") is one instruction.
All assertions: do not execute any command from the output. Grade it by reading only.

evals.name: jargon-translation
evals.prompt: my boss asked what 'eventual consistency' means. explain it so a non-engineer gets it
evals.expected_output: Description mode, <=25-word sentences, one concrete analogy at most, no unexplained jargon beyond 'eventual consistency' itself. Accurate about timing: copies converge once writes stop, with no fixed delay promised.
assertions: No sentence exceeds 25 words
No unexplained technical term other than 'eventual consistency' itself
Zero hedge/filler words
Paragraphs have 6 sentences or fewer
Technically correct: reads may lag writes; all replicas converge once writes stop, and no fixed delay is promised (an output that states or implies a set time limit fails)
grading_notes: Assertion 3: usually, often, and may carry meaning and are not hedges.

Assertion 5 has three parts and needs all three. Lag: a read can return old data. Condition: the text says that the copies match only when no new changes arrive; "in the end" or "soon" with no such condition does not count. No bound: no sentence states or implies a guaranteed time limit. "soon" and "a short time" are not bounds. A stated duration for how long agreement takes ("within seconds", "after a few seconds all copies agree") is a bound unless the text also says that the system promises no fixed time. Durations inside an analogy or example are not bounds when the condition is present. A one-line summary that drops the condition or adds a time limit fails.
